subject: Post-call: Acme — batching & concurrency assumptions / pricing follow-up
messages:
From: Camila Reyes <camila@redwood.com>
To: Sarah Chen <sarah.chen@acme.com>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa@redwood.com>, Aditya Rao <aditya@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-08-15T14:12:00-07:00
Subject: Post-call recap — batching & concurrency assumptions / next steps

Hi Sarah — great to meet earlier. Quick recap and open items from today's discovery so we can size pricing and recommend batching/concurrency knobs: 

Summary of what you shared
- Primary workload: customer support summarization + classification for chat transcripts
- Average input length ~600 tokens (post-cleaning), average output ~120 tokens
- Expected steady-state QPS: ~8-12 r/s (business hours), peak bursts up to ~40 concurrent requests for short windows
- Monthly forecast: range 100M-200M prompt+completion tokens (you said 150M as a mid)

Key follow-ups we promised
1) Confirm target unit economics (you mentioned a target in the ~$800–$1,000 per 1M tokens area) — please confirm target $/1M tokens and any formal budget range.
2) Share workload CSV (samples + token distribution) — we can use this to simulate continuous-batching benefits.
3) Align on tolerance for latency vs cost — eg. 250ms p50 target vs aggressive batching that increases p95.
4) Introduce Marissa (our SE) to scope a short throughput/latency runbook and PoC.

Batching / concurrency assumptions (early thoughts)
- Continuous batching model fits well for a steady QPS workload like yours; we typically see 20-40% token-cost reduction vs naively treating each request independently, depending on sequence-length variance and cache hit rate.
- With average request size (~720 combined tokens) and the peaks you described, we'd recommend testing with target batch windows of 10-30ms and concurrency headroom to allow opportunistic batching.
- For peak bursts (40 concurrent), we'd recommend a mix of pre-warmed burst capacity + fallback to slightly lower-cost model variants for non-critical requests.

Attachments: I'm attaching a blank workload template and our pricing model (redwood_pricing_model_v2.xlsx). If you can drop your workload summary into the template that will let us produce a 1M-token unit-econ example tuned to your distribution.

Next steps
- Sarah: share workload CSV and confirm target $/1M tokens and budget window
- Camila/Marissa/Aditya: run sims and come back with 2 pricing scenarios (PoC/Prod) + recommended batch/concurrency config
- Optional: 30-min follow-up next week for Marissa to walk through throughput assumptions (proposed Wed 8/19 10am PT)

Thanks — Camila

--

Thanks Camila — appreciate the clear recap. Confirming details from our side and attaching the workload summary you requested.

Quick answers:
- Monthly token range: 120M-180M (we're comfortable modeling at 150M as a baseline)
- Avg tokens per request: ~600 prompt + ~120 completion (~720 total)
- Peak concurrent requests: short bursts up to ~40, sustained concurrency target is ~12-15 during business hours
- Latency tolerance: p50 < 250ms is ideal for the product team; p95 can be up to 800-900ms for non-live actions (we can tolerate some tail).
- Budget: we are targeting ~$900 per 1M tokens for the initial contract window; total monthly budget target for inference is ~$135k–$170k depending on unit econ assumptions.

Attaching: acme_workload_summary.pdf (includes sample requests and token distribution).

Question: on the continuous batching assumptions — do you expect we should tune our client-side timeout to encourage slightly larger batch formation (eg. 15-20ms) or does Redwood handle batching server-side transparently without client changes?

Sarah

Subject: Re: Post-call recap — batching & concurrency assumptions / next steps

Thanks Sarah — this is perfect and very helpful. I pulled a couple quick numbers and a short unit-econ example below so we can align before Marissa runs a throughput sim.

Short answers first: 
- Redwood handles continuous batching server-side by default (no client changes required). That said, small client-side batching windows (10-20ms) can increase effective batch sizes for very low-latency callers and are an easy knob if you want to bias toward cost savings.

Unit-econ example (back-of-envelope) — using your baseline 150M tokens and target $900 / 1M tokens:
- Target price per token = $900 / 1,000,000 = $0.0009 per token
- Monthly cost at target rate = 150,000,000 * 0.0009 = $135,000

Effect of continuous batching (example assumptions)
- Baseline (no batching): per-token inference cost X (model+gpu) — we normalize to baseline price A
- With continuous batching and KV/prefix caching for repeated prompts we typically observe 20-35% reduction in effective token execution (depends on variance). With your distribution (avg 720 tokens, modest variance) Marissa expects ~25-30% token-efficiency improvement in an initial run.
- If we apply 25% improvement: effective billed tokens = 150M * 0.75 = 112.5M => monthly cost = 112,500,000 * 0.0009 = $101,250 (example).

Concurrency notes and recommended config
- For steady-state 12-15 concurrency, continuous batching will maximize GPU throughput without hurting p50 latency.
- For peaks (~40 concurrent), we'll rely on a short pre-warmed burst pool and fallback routing to a compatible, slightly less expensive model variant for best-effort requests (non-critical classification).
- Marissa will propose: batch window 10-30ms, per-model concurrency cap, and a burst policy (pre-warm + soft-failover) for spikes.

Next steps
- Marissa: can you take the attached workload and run a 2-scenario sim (conservative/optimistic batching) and produce an expected cost table + recommended batch window?
- Sarah: confirm decision-makers for procurement (names + emails) so we can loop in pricing/procurement.
- Camila: I'll book Wed 8/19 10am PT for a 30-min deep-dive with Marissa unless you propose another time.

I'll attach a cleaned pricing model after Marissa's sim but the quick B/E above shows we're in the ballpark of your $900 / 1M target if batching realizes ~25% efficiency.

Cheers — Camila
